title: Priya's Perfect Plan Goes Wild
markdown:
The Moonlit Book Festival had been pinned to Priya’s clipboard for six weeks, and she meant every pin. Lanterns hung in measured rows along the lakeside path. Programmes lay in a ribboned stack that refused to sit still. Priya the lynx, sandy-furred and late-night precise, tapped a claw on the timetable as if the paper itself might try to wander.

“Everything is just right, Bea,” she said. “The lemonade is chilled. The poets are ready. The sign for the Enchanting Elves of Eldoria reading is centred.”

Bea the goat, wool still rumpled from a morning roll, hummed a wobbly bleat and watched a programme lift, settle, lift again. She had come as Priya’s reminder that a festival, like a field, grew better when it was not clipped into boxes.

Then Professor Alistair Grimshaw arrived, spectacles flashing, and read the Elves of Eldoria sign as if it had personally insulted Rome.

“This is a joke, I presume,” he said, dry as old paper. “I am here to discuss the Roman Empire. Not elves.”

Priya’s whiskers drooped. Before she could produce the colour-coded defence, a gust smelling of ink and excitement brought Alwen Button, children’s author, bouncing in tweed toward the Lakeside Pavilion.

“Ah! Perfect for my Exploding Jellybeans reading!” Alwen boomed, and beamed at the professor, who flinched as if jellybeans were a barbarian tribe.

Hard on his heels came the avant-garde poets in black and silver. Their leader, Zephyr, hair like spun moonlight, glided forward.

“The moon calls to us,” Zephyr whispered. “This pavilion shall be our sanctuary for Echoes in the Obsidian. We sense profound resonance.”

Three appointments. One pavilion. Two o’clock, three o’clock, four o’clock — all now trying to occupy the same slice of moon.

“There must be a mistake,” Priya said, voice too tight, lavender sachets doing nothing for her paws. “Professor Grimshaw at two, Alwen Button at three, the poets at four. We have plenty of time for each.”

Alwen was already debating with Zephyr about whether jellybeans could explode in iambic pentameter. The professor tapped his watch. The poets began a low atmospheric chant that wove through the leaves like a second, unofficial programme.

Bea nudged Priya’s shoulder. “Perhaps the elves, the jellybeans, and the echoes can all share the moonlight. It’s a rather large pavilion, and the moon is quite generous.”

Priya looked from clipboard to crowd. The plan was in pieces. The pieces, inconveniently, were smiling. A daring thought took root where the spontaneity buffer zone had been a joke in the margin.

“We are not losing control,” she declared, and the words arrived warmer than she had packed them. “We are broadening the interpretation.”

Because she said it aloud, it became a schedule of a different kind. Professor Grimshaw, after an unexpectedly interesting chat with Zephyr about how empires and poems both fade and endure, began weaving historical parallels through his lecture. He spoke of the fall of cities as if they were stanzas, and even Alwen Button scribbled notes, then gave the jellybeans a touch of historical flair — a confectionary uprising, a sweet republic, a fizz that made the professor’s frown twitch toward something almost like amusement. The poets, sensing the audience’s delight, found their Obsidian Echoes resonating with new depth, as if Rome and sugar and moonlight had been waiting in the same pavilion all along.

The programmes, at last, sat still. The ribbon held.

As the moon climbed, Bea munched and nudged again. “Joy doesn’t always come in neat boxes, Priya. Sometimes it spills, and that’s when it’s most delicious.”

Priya watched Grimshaw, Alwen, and Zephyr share a single lantern’s circle, none of them on time and all of them, somehow, on purpose. The most enchanting part of her plan had not been the precision. It had been the moment she gave everyone permission to add a spark.

And so the lynx who loved a perfect timetable learned that a generous moon can hold more than one reading at once, and that a plan is strongest when it leaves room for the unexpected page.
characters: Priya (lynx late-night radio producer), Bea (goat flatmate)
